features.title: Member roster and roles
features.summary: The host-local member roster of each Workspace: where it is kept and how it is protected, members with their kinds and cumulative roles, bootstrapping a first Owner, carrying a roster over to a moved Workspace, and managing it from the CLI and the Workbench.

rules.statement: Each Workspace has exactly one roster on the host, identified by the real path of its root, so a symlink and its target share it; no roster serves two Workspaces, so the same person in two Workspaces is two independent members, possibly with different roles.

A roster lives only on the host, under `$UIUX_HOME`, never in the Workspace or in Git, and it changes no canonical file, manifest field or `schemaVersion`; a copy of a Workspace therefore carries no members or credentials.
UIUX refuses a roster store that is a symlink, that is writable by group or others, or that records a Workspace root other than the one being served, and never silently reuses such a store.
Every roster write is atomic under the store's lock.

The CLI and a running server may both write a roster: the server re-reads it when it changes, at the check interval the Access Contract sets, so a CLI revoke, removal or role change takes effect on its next request without a restart.
A member's kind, human or Agent, is fixed at creation, so an Agent can never be turned into a human to gain human-only powers.
A member's nickname is unique in its roster, ignoring case, and is its display name everywhere.
An Owner may rename a member or change its role; records written earlier keep the name they were written with.
Roles are cumulative, Viewer ⊂ Reviewer ⊂ Editor ⊂ Owner: each role may do everything the roles below it may do (the Access Contract lists which operations need which role).
Agents are capped at Editor, so minting credentials and changing roles stay with humans: an Agent can never be made Owner.
A roster's last human Owner cannot be removed or demoted.
Removing a member also removes its Tokens, invites and sessions, so none of them works after the server's next roster reload.

When `uiux dev` opens a roster that has no human Owner, it creates one named after the sanitized OS user name (falling back to `owner`) and prints an invite sign-in link for it with the loopback URL and the commands for adding an Agent.
Later starts print no bootstrap link, and startup never prints a Token.

UIUX does not detect a moved or renamed Workspace or a git worktree: a Workspace at a new real path starts with an empty roster and bootstraps its own Owner, unless an old roster is carried over with `uiux access copy`.

A copied roster is independent of its source: it records the new Workspace root and gets its own roster hint, it carries no invites, sessions or last-used times, and later changes in either roster never reach the other.
The roster's recorded Workspace root and hint are shown in the `uiux dev` startup output, by `uiux member list` and on the Workbench Members page.

On the loopback listener, a signed-in human Owner manages the served Workspace's roster on the Workbench Members page: adding, renaming, changing the role of and removing members, creating Tokens (with a copy action) and revoking them, creating invites, and listing and revoking sessions.
The Workbench hides the actions the signed-in member's role cannot perform, or disables them and names the required role; the server stays the authority.

features.title: Authentication and credentials
features.summary: Authentication of every `/api/*` and `/mcp` request: member Tokens, invites and sessions and how browsers and Agents use them, their lifetimes, revocation and failure handling, and the system credentials of internal readers.

rules.statement: Every `/api/*` and `/mcp` request authenticates with a credential, loopback included; only the public routes, which carry no Workspace data, need none. There is no unauthenticated mode.

Every request resolves to at most one principal, the member or system credential it authenticates as, and a member's current role is resolved on every request: a credential carries no scope of its own, so a role change, removal or revocation applies at once.
A browser signs in on `/login` with a single-use invite link or a pasted member Token and receives a fresh session; a Token used to sign in stays valid.
An invite link carries the invite in its URL fragment, which the sign-in page removes after reading it.
The browser on the host is not implicitly the Owner: it signs in like every other browser.
Agents and scripts authenticate with member Tokens, so no web page can drive MCP with ambient browser credentials.
A credential is valid only on the server of the Workspace whose roster issued it: the server looks its public ID up in its own roster and verifies it by hash.
The roster hint inside a credential never decides its validity, so Tokens carried over by `uiux access copy` keep working.
Only hashes of credentials are stored, and each credential's plaintext is shown once, when it is created.
A Token, invite or session stops working when its lifetime, set by the Access Contract, runs out; a Token may instead be created with another expiry or explicitly with none.
Tokens, invites and sessions survive server restarts.
Invites sign browsers in and are issued only for human members; Agents get Tokens.

A Token ends when it is revoked, expires or its member is removed; a session ends on sign-out, Owner revocation, member removal or expiry. Either takes effect on the server's next request, which is then refused as unauthenticated, and the Workbench returns to `/login`.

A malformed, unknown, expired or revoked credential is refused with one failure code, so a response never reveals whether a credential was revoked; a credential from another Workspace's roster gets the same code with a message that names both rosters.
Repeated authentication failures from one remote address are rate-limited, at the limit the Access Contract sets.
The rate limit counts distinct failed credentials per address, so one stale credential retried by a client does not lock the address out, and the in-memory system credentials are never rate-limited.
Secrets never appear in logs: `Authorization` headers, session cookies and credential-shaped strings are redacted.
The server records when each Token and session was last used and writes that to the roster at a bounded interval that the Access Contract sets.

A session belongs to the origin where it was created, so `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` and a LAN address each need their own sign-in, and two `uiux dev` servers on one host never overwrite each other's session; every sign-in mints a fresh session.
Formal capture and `uiux publish` read the live server with random, per-process system credentials that are not members and act with Viewer scope.
System credentials are never stored, logged or stamped as actors.
The server counts rejected `/mcp` attempts in memory (time, user agent and listener), and the Owner sees an "MCP clients without a token" notice that offers to create a Token for an Agent.
The Workbench header shows the signed-in member's nickname and role with a sign-out action.

features.title: Baseline request gates
features.summary: The baseline request gates (Host, Origin, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, Content-Type and framing) that run on every listener before authentication, and what each of them refuses.

rules.statement: The baseline request gates (Host, Origin, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, Content-Type and framing) run first on every listener, ahead of every handler including static assets; authentication runs after them, and authorization in the shared application layer.
A request whose `Host` is not on the Host allowlist of the listener that accepted it is refused before any handler runs; the Access Contract gives each listener's allowlist.
The LAN listener checks `Host` against its own allowlist, not the loopback listener's.

A state-changing request and every `/mcp` request are refused when they carry an `Origin` other than the server's own origin, or a `Sec-Fetch-Site` outside the allowed values; the Access Contract defines state-changing methods and those values.
On the loopback listener, a request without an `Origin`, such as one from a script or an MCP client, is not refused for lacking it.
On the LAN listener a state-changing request must carry an `Origin` equal to the LAN origin; a missing `Origin` is refused like a foreign one.
A state-changing request that carries a body must declare `Content-Type: application/json`.
UIUX never sends CORS headers.
Every response forbids framing by other origins, while the Workbench can still frame its own same-origin Preview.
Running the packaged server directly applies the same loopback-only bind policy as `uiux dev`.

features.title: LAN reviewer access
features.summary: The opt-in LAN listener through which human members on other devices, and Agents with LAN-enabled Tokens, reach the same server: its trust model, credentials, transport security and plain-HTTP warning.

rules.statement: LAN access is an opt-in second listener into the same server and application layer; the loopback listener behaves exactly as it does without it.
Listener-specific policy follows the listener that accepted the connection, never the client's source address.
A LAN request is authenticated like a loopback request, and the member's role decides what it may do; the LAN listener has no route allowlist of its own, so an Editor may author over the LAN.
Member, Token, invite and session administration is never served on the LAN listener, so no credential is created or shown over it.
A Token works on the LAN listener, for `/mcp`, `/api/*` or signing in, only if it was created with the LAN flag; a default Token is loopback-only, so an everyday Token never crosses the LAN.
Without TLS the LAN listener serves plain HTTP; with both TLS flags it serves HTTPS.

When the LAN listener serves plain HTTP, UIUX shows a non-dismissible warning that anyone on the network can capture sign-in links, session cookies and LAN Tokens and reuse them; with TLS no warning is shown.
The plain-HTTP warning appears next to the LAN URLs at startup, with the number of LAN-enabled Tokens, in the output of `uiux token create --lan`, and on the sign-in and Members pages on LAN origins.
With the LAN listener running, startup prints each reachable LAN URL.
Formal capture keeps loading Preview from the internal loopback origin and never uses the LAN listener.
The Workbench works on a plain-HTTP LAN origin, which is not a secure context: copying text and generating identifiers do not depend on secure-context-only browser APIs.

features.title: Agent edit leases
features.summary: Short-lived, per-resource edit leases that Agents take on what they write: which resources are leased, how leases are taken, renewed, checked and released, how they relate to revision checks, and how the Workbench shows them.

rules.statement: Edit leases cover Views, UX Flows, Locales, authored Assets and the Workspace settings, one lease per resource; Review threads are never leased.
A lease is held by a member and lives only in server memory. Leases are fail-fast: a writer never waits or queues for one.
A lease expires a fixed duration, set by the Access Contract, after its holder's last successful write to that resource or explicit acquire; the duration cannot be set per call.

A mutation by any principal that would write a resource leased by another member is refused before the domain write, with no side effects. This includes promoting a Review to a Decision, which writes the View.
A successful write by an Agent member to an unleased resource, a create included, takes its lease; a human's writes only check leases and never take one.
Every successful write by the holder renews its lease on that resource, and so does acquiring it again.
The lease check and a tentative reservation happen before the write, and a write that fails (for example on a conflict, invalid input or a blocked precondition) never leaves a new lease behind.
A lease ends when its holder releases it, when it expires, when an Owner force-releases it, when its holder is removed or loses the Editor role, or when the server restarts.
An Owner is not exempt from another member's lease: writing the resource needs an explicit, visible force-release first.

A lease coordinates and never replaces revision checks: the holder still sends `expectedRevision`, a lease never turns a conflict into success, and writes made outside UIUX ignore leases but are still caught by revision checks.

The lease Tools and the per-request MCP instructions describe the recipe for long Agent tasks: acquire every resource the task will write up front, re-acquire as a heartbeat before a long pause such as a build or capture, and release all leases at the end.

The Workbench shows "Locked by <nickname>" with the expiry on a leased resource and disables its edit controls with that reason; an Owner gets a release action, and a lease refusal shows the same message inline and keeps the user's draft.

features.title: Server-stamped actors
features.summary: Server-stamped actors and times on Review records written through `/api/*` and `/mcp`: what is stamped, how caller-supplied values are treated, and what a stamp guarantees.

rules.statement: On `/api/*` and `/mcp`, every timeline-writing Review mutation (reply, re-anchor, mark ready, resolve, reopen and message edit) takes its actor from the authenticated member, never from the request.
The Decision provenance written by promoting a Review thread takes its actor from the authenticated member as well.
A request-supplied `actor` is optional and ignored: when it differs from the stamp, the write still succeeds and the result carries a warning.

The authored time of those records is the server's clock: a supplied `at` is ignored with a warning, while in-process callers of the domain services, such as tests and migration, still pass their own.

Stamping never rewrites history: records written before keep their caller-asserted actors, and a removed member's records keep its member ID and recorded display name, which the Workbench marks as removed.
A stamp shows that the write came through a credential issued to that member, not who held the credential.

features.title: MCP surface and discovery
features.summary: How Agents discover and read a Workspace over MCP: the split between Resources and Tools, Resource addressing, compact discovery results, a role-independent Tool list, and the per-request instructions.

rules.statement: MCP Resources are the point-read surface for directly addressable read models; discovery, filtering, search and listing are read-only Tools, and every mutation and imperative action (such as formal capture, Handoff export and Review actions) is a Tool.

MCP Resource URIs address resources by kind and canonical key within the one Workspace the server was started for: they are stable within that server, carry no Workspace identity, and are not portable Handoff identities.
List and search results are compact and paginated: full bodies and large artifacts are read through Resources instead of being copied into Tool results.
List and search can expand their compact items with more detail or selected fields on explicit request.

Each MCP request's server instructions tell the Agent which member it is authenticated as and that Review actors and times are stamped by the server, so an Agent learns its identity without an extra Tool.
Every tool stays registered whatever the caller's role, so the tool list never changes with the role; a tool the role cannot use refuses with the role refusal, which names the required role.

features.title: Static publication
features.summary: The read-only static publication of one Workspace that `uiux publish` builds: what it contains and leaves out, its independence from a server, its content identity and provenance, and where it can be hosted.

rules.statement: `uiux publish` builds a portable, read-only interactive site of one Workspace that needs no UIUX server, MCP or filesystem access at runtime: the canonical resources, the Preview Adapter runtime, Assets, formal Evidence artifacts and the Workspace Handoff readiness assessment are captured at build time.
Authoring controls are removed from the published site, while View context switching, Preview, the Inspector, UX Flows, Evidence inspection and readiness stay interactive.
The publication carries no Review threads: its Handoff readiness assessment may show aggregate Review counts (per resolution and unresolved) but no thread IDs or links to threads.
Publication output carries a deterministic content identity and, when a source revision is given, that revision as provenance.
The published site works under the URL path given as its base (default `/`), such as a GitHub Pages project subpath.
Publication output contains no access data: no members, credentials or roster information.
Building a publication never creates or reads a host roster: the internal server it reads from keeps an empty in-memory roster and accepts only the run's own publish system credential.

features.title: Live refresh
features.summary: Server-pushed change notifications that keep open Workbenches current, how clients resynchronize or fall back, and how the Workbench treats remote changes and revision conflicts while a user works.

rules.statement: The server pushes change notifications to Workbenches over a server-sent events stream open to every authenticated member on both listeners.
After each successful commit to a View, UX Flow, Locale, Review thread, Asset or the Workspace, the stream sends a change or removal event for that resource.
The stream also sends an event when a lease is acquired, released or force-released, and when the roster or the member's role changes.
Events never carry canonical content, actors or message bodies; clients re-read what changed through the normal point-read and list APIs.
Nothing is replayed: `Last-Event-ID` is ignored, and a reconnect, or a changed server instance ID after a restart, makes the client resynchronize what it shows from canonical resources.
Commits made through `/api/*` and `/mcp` emit alike, because both run in the same server process; edits made to Workspace files outside UIUX are not detected.
When the event stream cannot connect, the Workbench falls back to polling.
The server caps the open event streams per session, and ending a session closes its open stream.
When an on-screen resource changes elsewhere and the user has no draft of it, the Workbench re-reads and re-renders it without asking and briefly highlights new timeline entries.

When it changes while the user is drafting, the Workbench keeps the draft, re-reads and shows an "updated by others" notice above the composer; the draft's `expectedRevision` moves to the fresh revision only when the user acknowledges the notice.

After a revision conflict the Workbench never resends or retries a write by itself: it re-reads, keeps the draft or choices and shows the new state, and the user acts again, so an action aimed at one state never silently applies to a newer one.

contracts.title: Mutation and revision semantics
contracts.summary: The semantics every canonical mutation shares on every transport (`/api/*`, `/mcp` and the Workbench): opaque content-derived revisions, the required `expectedRevision`, all-or-nothing conflicts that report the current revision, compact mutation results, the meaning of refusal statuses, how the shared result surfaces over HTTP and MCP, and the change events that commits emit to Workbenches.

clauses.statement: Every mutable canonical resource has an opaque revision derived from its canonical content. Reads and queries return it; it is the same across process restarts and changes whenever that content changes, including through an edit made outside UIUX. Callers must not infer meaning from its representation.
Every mutation of an existing resource carries the `expectedRevision` its caller last read for that resource; a Review action carries its thread's.
A create carries no `expectedRevision`. It names or receives the identity of the new resource, and when a resource with that identity already exists it writes nothing and returns `already_exists`.

When the resource's current revision differs from `expectedRevision`, the whole mutation writes nothing and returns a `conflict` result carrying `currentRevision`; the caller must re-read and decide again.

A successful mutation returns its status, `created`, `updated` or `deleted`, and the affected identity. `created` and `updated` also return the new revision and diagnostics; `deleted`, the result of retracting a Review thread, carries no revision. A result never carries the whole Workspace.
A successful mutation result also carries a summary of what changed.
Competing writes are never merged automatically, by implicit merge, CRDT or OT: the later writer gets a conflict and must re-read, retry or rework explicitly.

Refusals are told apart by status: `conflict` means re-read, `blocked` means a precondition refuses the operation, and `locked` means another member holds an edit lease on the resource, so retry later or ask the holder.
A lease refusal is `{ status: "locked", key, code: "resource.locked", message, lock: { kind, key, holder: { nickname, kind }, expiresAt } }`; it names the holder only by nickname and member kind.
A persistence-busy refusal has the code `persistence.busy`; over HTTP it answers 503 with a `Retry-After` header.
Over HTTP the structured result is the JSON response body; `conflict` and `already_exists` answer 409, and `locked` answers 423.
Over MCP a tool returns the structured result as its structured content (and as JSON text), and any outcome other than success is an error result (`isError`).
HTTP and MCP run an operation through the same application service and return the same result for it; only the transport envelope differs.

The change-event stream is the server-sent events route `GET /api/events`. On connect it sends `hello` with the server instance ID; it sends `resource.changed` (kind, key, revision) or `resource.removed` (kind, key) for a resource, `lock.changed` (kind, key) for a lease and `access.changed` for the roster or the member's role, and a heartbeat comment about every 20 seconds.

contracts.title: MCP interface
contracts.summary: The Model Context Protocol surface that Agents use against one selected Workspace: the `/mcp` endpoint and its bearer authentication, the read-only Resources, the discovery, authoring, Review, Evidence, Handoff and lease Tools, and the per-request instructions.

clauses.statement: MCP is served at `/mcp` on the selected Workspace's `uiux dev` server.
A `/mcp` request reaches a Tool or Resource only with a valid member Token.

On `/mcp`, the message of an authentication failure names the fix: create a Token with `uiux token create` and send it as a bearer Token, or, for a Token of another Workspace's roster, create one for this Workspace or run `uiux access copy`.
UIUX advertises no OAuth metadata: every `/.well-known/*` path answers a JSON 404.
On the LAN listener `/mcp` refuses a Token created without the LAN flag with HTTP 403 `auth.lan_not_allowed`.
The per-request server instructions begin with "Authenticated as <nickname> (<kind>, <role>)." for the authenticated member.

MCP Resources are read-only: the selected Workspace, each View, UX Flow, Locale, Review thread and authored Asset by its canonical key, and each derived artifact by its `sha256:` digest. Reading one that does not exist is a not-found error.

`list_resources` lists, and `search_resources` searches with a non-empty query, the Views, UX Flows, Locales, Review threads and authored Assets, optionally filtered by kind and, for Review threads, by resolution and anchor scope. Both take a required page `limit` and an opaque `cursor`, and each item carries its kind, key, revision, diagnostic count, a kind-specific summary and its Resource URI.

`create_view` creates a View with the canonical empty RootShell IR, no Variants and no Decisions; `update_view_spec` replaces the descriptive Spec fields, keeping Decisions and every non-Spec field; `update_view_structure` replaces the IR and Variants together, keeping the View's identity, name, `feature` tag and Spec.
`update_workspace_settings` updates the manifest-owned Workspace settings (`i18n.defaultLocale`, `adapters`, `viewports` and `themes`) and keeps `schemaVersion`.
`create_locale` creates a Locale file named by a canonical BCP 47 tag and fails if it exists; `update_locale` updates an existing Locale's messages.
`create_flow` creates a UX Flow (identity, entry step and step transition graph) and fails if it exists; `update_flow` updates one, keeping its identity.
`create_asset` creates an authored Asset from its metadata and source content; `replace_asset` replaces an authored Asset, keeping its identity.

The Review tools are `create_review_thread`, `append_review_message`, `reanchor_review_thread`, `set_review_display_hint`, `submit_ready_for_review`, `reopen_review_thread`, `promote_review_to_decision`, `edit_review_message` and `retract_review_thread`; each atomically changes one Review thread (promotion also writes the target View's Decisions).

`resolve_review_thread` stays registered but always refuses: a human member gets `review.resolve_requires_workbench`, an Agent asking for a resolution other than `verified` gets `review.direct_resolve_requires_workbench`, and any other Agent gets `review.resolve_requires_human`.

`capture_formal_evidence` captures formal Evidence for an explicit list of resolved render contexts; `assess_handoff_readiness` assesses explicit Handoff roots without exporting; `export_handoff` exports an immutable Handoff bundle from explicit roots.

`acquire_lock` takes `{ resources: [{ kind, key }] }` with 1 to 16 entries and is all-or-nothing: it returns `{ status: "acquired", leases: [{ kind, key, expiresAt }] }`, or `locked` naming every conflicting lease. `release_lock` takes optional `resources` (omitted means all of the caller's leases), is idempotent and returns the released list.

contracts.title: Access control
contracts.summary: Authentication and authorization on every UIUX server surface: the host-local roster store, member records, credential formats and hashing, the session cookie, public routes, which credential each surface accepts, authentication and gate refusals, the permission matrix by role, the session and administration routes, and the stamped actor value.

clauses.statement: A Workspace's roster is the file `$UIUX_HOME/workspaces/<wsid>/access.json`, where `<wsid>` is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the Workspace root's real path.

The roster file is a JSON object `{ version: 1, workspaceRoot, hint, members, tokens, invites, sessions }`, where `workspaceRoot` is the Workspace root's real path and `hint` is 4 random lowercase base32 characters chosen when the roster is created.
The roster store's directories have mode 0700 and the roster file has mode 0600, so only the host user can access them.
A running server checks its roster for changes at most once per second, and writes each Token's or session's last-used time to the roster at most once a minute.

A member record is `{ id, nickname, kind, role, createdAt }`: `id` is a full UUID, `nickname` matches `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,31}$`, `kind` is `human` or `agent`, and `role` is `owner`, `editor`, `reviewer` or `viewer`.
Removing or demoting a roster's last human Owner is refused with `auth.last_owner`.

Tokens, invites and sessions are strings `uiux_t_<hint>_<id>_<secret>`, `uiux_i_<hint>_<id>_<secret>` and `uiux_s_<hint>_<id>_<secret>`, all lowercase RFC 4648 base32 (`a-z2-7`): `<hint>` is the roster hint, `<id>` is the 10-character public ID used for lookup, listing and revocation, and `<secret>` is 52 characters encoding 32 random bytes.
A stored hash is `sha256:` followed by the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the full credential string, and verification compares it in constant time.
Credential lifetimes are 90 days for a member Token, 24 hours for an invite, and, for a session, 14 days idle or 30 days in total.
The system credentials are `system:capture` for formal capture and `system:publish` for `uiux publish`.
The browser session cookie is `uiux_session_<hint>` (with the roster hint), set with `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/`, plus `Secure` under TLS.
These routes need no credential: `GET /api/health`, the SPA documents and `/_nuxt/*` assets (static code with no Workspace data), the `/login` page, `POST /api/session/login`, and `/.well-known/*`.
The Nuxt Icon collection endpoint `/api/_nuxt_icon/*`, which serves static icon data and no Workspace data, is public as well.

A session cookie is accepted on `/api/*` and for Preview data but never on `/mcp`; a member Token sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` is accepted on `/api/*` and required on `/mcp`; a system credential is accepted only on the read routes of `/api/*` and Preview data.

A missing credential is `401 auth.required`; a malformed, unknown, expired or revoked credential, or one from another Workspace's roster, is `401 auth.invalid_credential`. Authentication failures are limited to 10 per minute per remote address, and a rate-limited attempt is `429 auth.rate_limited`. A 401 carries `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="uiux"`.

A role refusal is `auth.scope_denied` with the required role: over HTTP a 403 with the body `{ status: "blocked", code: "auth.scope_denied", requiredRole, message, diagnostics }`, over MCP a tool error result with the same structured content.

Baseline gate refusals are `421 request.host_rejected` for a foreign `Host`, `403 request.origin_rejected` for a foreign `Origin`, `403 request.cross_site_rejected` for a disallowed `Sec-Fetch-Site` and `415 request.content_type_rejected` for a non-JSON state-changing body; every response carries `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'` and `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`.
The loopback listener's Host allowlist is `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` and `[::1]` on the bound port; the LAN listener's is its bound IP literals and the `--lan-hostname` values on the LAN port.
The safe methods are GET, HEAD and OPTIONS; a request with any other method is state-changing.
The allowed `Sec-Fetch-Site` values are `same-origin` and `none`.

Viewer may read: Resources, `list_resources`, `search_resources` and `assess_handoff_readiness` on MCP; `GET /api/resources/:kind/:key`, `POST /api/resources/list` and `/search`, artifacts, Asset content, the Evidence list, the publication snapshot, Preview data, `POST /api/handoff/assess`, `GET /api/events` and `GET /api/locks` on HTTP; and the matching Workbench browsing.

Reviewer adds every Review action: creating a thread, replying, re-anchoring, setting or clearing the pin hint, marking ready, reopening, promoting to a Decision, editing one's own message and retracting one's own new thread, on MCP (`create_review_thread`, `append_review_message`, `reanchor_review_thread`, `set_review_display_hint`, `submit_ready_for_review`, `reopen_review_thread`, `promote_review_to_decision`, `edit_review_message`, `retract_review_thread`) and on the matching `/api/reviews` routes, plus resolving in the Workbench.

Editor adds authoring of Views, Workspace settings, Locales, UX Flows and Assets (`create_view`, `update_view_spec`, `update_view_structure`, `update_workspace_settings`, `create_locale`, `update_locale`, `create_flow`, `update_flow`, `create_asset`, `replace_asset` and their HTTP routes), formal capture (`capture_formal_evidence`, `POST /api/evidence/capture`), Handoff export (`export_handoff`, `POST /api/handoff/export`) and edit leases (`acquire_lock`, `release_lock`).

Owner adds member, Token, invite and session administration (`/api/access/members`, `/api/access/tokens`, `/api/access/invites`, `/api/access/sessions` and `GET /api/access/mcp-attempts`), allowed only to a human Owner on a cookie session on the loopback listener, and force-releasing a lease (`DELETE /api/locks/:kind/:key`), allowed to a human Owner on a cookie session on either listener.

`POST /api/reviews/:id/resolve` requires a human member with the Reviewer role or above on a cookie session: a bearer Token is refused with `review.resolve_requires_workbench`, and an Agent's session with `review.resolve_requires_human`.

`POST /api/session/login` with `{ credential }` (an invite or a member Token) sets the session cookie and returns `{ member: { id, nickname, kind, role } }`; `GET /api/session` returns the current member and `DELETE /api/session` signs out, both for cookie sessions only.
`GET /api/locks` lists the current leases as `{ kind, key, holder: { nickname, kind }, expiresAt }`.
The edit-lease duration is five minutes.
A stamped actor is `{ type: <member kind>, id: "member:<member id>", displayName: <nickname> }`.
A request-supplied `actor` that differs from the stamp yields the warning `auth.actor_ignored`, and a supplied `at` yields the warning `auth.time_ignored`.

## Notes

- Why a Contract: authentication and authorization cut across every server surface and Feature, and the host-local store and credential formats have their own version (`version: 1`) independent of the Workspace schema.
- There is no HTTP Contract (owner ruling Q4); the HTTP routes named here are the ones whose access rules are normative.
- `<wsid>` in the store path is the hex SHA-256 of the Workspace root's real path; `<hint>` in credentials and the cookie name is the roster's 4-character hint. They are different values.
- A principal is what a request authenticates as: a member, or a system credential ({{R.access.credentials.current-role}}).
